::: {.kw-overview}
The unifying question this week is which kidneys are worth accepting, and for whom. An international target trial emulation spanning five European registries, the UK among them, finds that the survival advantage of a standard criteria donor kidney over continued dialysis holds at every recipient age, while the advantage of an expanded criteria kidney — particularly one retrieved after circulatory death — erodes as recipients get older, until at 75 it is statistically indistinguishable from staying on dialysis. Two papers attack the same problem from the assessment side and both counsel against easy answers: a very large systematic review finds that time-zero histology, for all its use in implant-or-discard decisions, rests on evidence of uniformly very low certainty, and a secondary analysis of a Dutch normothermic perfusion trial shows that the readouts most likely to be useful in real time, urine output and venous oxygen tension, are protocol-dependent and derived from too few kidneys to act on. Donor utilisation appears again in a US modelling study linking the curtailment of out-of-sequence allocation to several hundred kidneys that were never recovered, disproportionately the highest-risk organs, whose cold ischaemic times rose at the same time. Against that, the issue's only randomised trial is negative: complement blockade with eculizumab at the time of implantation did not reduce delayed graft function, leaving the field still without a licensed pharmacological option. The remaining three are the practical ones — an updated meta-analysis quantifying what ABO-incompatible transplantation costs in rejection and early bleeding against what it buys in graft survival, a two-centre series suggesting that routine prothrombin complex concentrate reversal of apixaban before implantation is unnecessary, and a French cohort showing that BK virus-specific T cell responses measured at the first detectable viraemia track who will clear the virus and who will need immunosuppression cut hard.
:::

---

### 1. [Survival benefit of deceased donor kidney transplantation versus continued dialysis: international target trial emulation](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100624)
[Hellemans R, Chesnaye NC, Kramer A, Fu EL, Arnol M, Åsberg A, Bistrup C, Ferraro PM, Heldal K, Helve J, Legeai C, Medcalf J, Nitsch D, Oliveras L, Pérez-Sáez MJ, Ponte B, Savoye E, Segelmark M, Shanmugaranjan S, Sørensen SS, Torra R, Ortiz A, Jager KJ, Stel VS. *BMJ*, 2026. PMID: 42759976.]{.kw-ref}

The survival benefit of transplantation over dialysis is the number every consultant quotes in clinic, and it is almost always quoted as a single figure when the honest answer depends on the recipient's age and on which kidney is being offered. This target trial emulation used European Renal Association Registry data from Catalonia, Denmark, France, Norway and the UK, taking 64,036 patients aged 20 or older who were on dialysis and waitlisted for a first deceased donor kidney-only transplant between 2000 and 2019, of whom 39,244 were transplanted, and comparing five-year patient survival after transplantation against continued dialysis within monthly sequential trials using flexible parametric spline models across recipient age. The transplanted organs split into 16,897 (43.1%) standard criteria donor kidneys retrieved after brain death, 4,324 (11.0%) standard criteria kidneys after circulatory death, 14,799 (37.7%) expanded criteria kidneys after brain death and 3,224 (8.2%) expanded criteria kidneys after circulatory death. Both standard criteria categories were associated with higher estimated five-year survival than continued dialysis at every recipient age, and the retrieval route made no material difference to that conclusion — a reassurance worth having in a programme as dependent on donation after circulatory death as the UK's. The expanded criteria categories behaved differently: their advantage narrowed as recipients aged, most steeply for expanded criteria kidneys retrieved after circulatory death, and among 75-year-olds the estimated five-year survival after such a transplant was 59% (95% confidence interval 51% to 66%) against 55% (54% to 55%) on continued dialysis, a hazard ratio of 0.97 (95% confidence interval 0.70 to 1.33) that held irrespective of diabetes or cardiovascular disease. That group also carried threefold higher early post-transplant mortality than their counterparts who stayed on dialysis, which locates the lost benefit in the perioperative period rather than in later graft failure. The authors are explicit that statistical uncertainty widens among the oldest recipients, so the finding is a narrowing of estimated benefit with a wide interval rather than a demonstration of equivalence, and registry emulation cannot fully remove confounding by the clinical judgement that put a given patient on the list in the first place. For a UK unit the practical consequence is in how an expanded criteria donation after circulatory death offer is discussed with a candidate in their mid-seventies: the conversation is no longer only about waiting time and graft longevity, but about an upfront mortality cost that this analysis suggests may not be recovered within five years.

### 2. [Declining allocation out of sequence is associated with fewer kidneys recovered and transplanted](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.09.020)
[Lin S, Delman AM, Martens GR, Marklin GF, Levanos T, Grinberg SZ, Doilicho NB, Yu J, Park Y, Vachharajani N, Alhamad T, Lovasik BP, Lindemann J, Cullinan DR, Khan AS, Doyle MB, Wellen JR, Ridley CH, Chapman WC, Lin Y. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42763039.]{.kw-ref}

Out-of-sequence placement is the mechanism by which a hard-to-place kidney reaches a centre willing to take it before the clock defeats it, and it is also the mechanism most exposed to the charge of circumventing the waiting list. Allocation out of sequence rose in the US after the KAS250 allocation change and then fell sharply from August 2024 under regulatory and public scrutiny; in 2025, deceased donor kidney recovery and transplant volume fell for the first time since KAS250, and the authors set out to test whether that fall exceeded what the shifting donor mix would predict. Because the donor pool had been moving towards higher kidney donor risk index organs, they fitted a donor-level model to the pre-August-2024 relationship between kidney donor risk index, donor type and seasonality on the one hand and kidney recovery on the other, then applied it to the donors actually observed afterwards to estimate expected recoveries. The model predicted 870 more kidney recoveries than occurred, and under a range of assumptions about how many recovered kidneys would go on to be used, that shortfall corresponds to roughly 360 to 630 transplants that did not happen. The declines were concentrated exactly where the concern would predict, in the highest kidney donor risk index kidneys, which also saw their cold ischaemic times lengthen over the same period. The authors are careful about what this design can and cannot show: the shortfall coincides with falling out-of-sequence allocation but could equally reflect unmeasured donor characteristics or any of the other changes running concurrently, and no causal claim is made. Its relevance to UK practice is not the allocation mechanism, which differs entirely, but the underlying tension it quantifies — NHS Blood and Transplant's fast-track and expedited placement routes exist for the same reason and attract the same equity objection, and this is the first national-scale estimate of what tightening such a pathway may cost in organs recovered rather than in organs fairly distributed.

### 3. [Time-Zero Kidney Biopsy and Deceased-Donor Transplant Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Prognostic Value, Prediction, and Clinical Utility](https://doi.org/10.3390/medsci14050566)
[Sainz-Bravo L, Gómez-Navarro B, Figueroa-Gamiño DL, Tapia-Báez JT, González-Barajas JD, Prieto-Magallanes ML, Solís-Rojas JÁ, Bautista-Reyes E, Gómez-Fregoso JA, De Arcos-Jiménez JC, Medina-González R, Camarena-Arteaga VA, Arizaga-Napoles M, Briseno-Ramirez J. *Med Sci (Basel)*, 2026. PMID: 42783439.]{.kw-ref}

Pre-implantation histology is used in many programmes as a tiebreaker on marginal kidneys, and this review is unusually disciplined in refusing to let four different questions collapse into one, keeping prognostic association, incremental prediction beyond clinical variables, clinical utility and measurement reproducibility separate throughout. The authors searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CENTRAL and three trial registries through 25 July 2026 with no date or language restriction, screening 25,746 of 45,676 retrieved records and including 203 eligible reports covering 159 study investigations and 154 cohort families, plus 22 contextual reports, taking one estimate per non-overlapping cohort under a prespecified hierarchy and pooling with random-effects restricted maximum likelihood models under Hartung-Knapp inference. Three associations reached conventional significance: vascular injury with delayed graft function (odds ratio 1.85, 95% CI 1.11–3.06), glomerulosclerosis with graft failure (hazard ratio 2.03, 1.22–3.39) and vascular injury with graft failure (hazard ratio 1.48, 1.07–2.04), while glomerulosclerosis and delayed graft function remained inconclusive (odds ratio 1.13, 0.59–2.17). The finding that matters more than any of those point estimates is that all twelve pooled bodies of evidence were graded very low certainty, which means the confidence intervals above understate the real uncertainty considerably. The authors' conclusion follows directly and is stated without hedging: current evidence does not support time-zero histology as a stand-alone rule for accepting or discarding a deceased donor kidney, and whether standardised histology adds anything beyond established clinical variables is an open question they argue should be settled in linked registry analyses before biopsy findings are allowed to guide management. Read against the preceding paper, the two point the same way from opposite directions — one shows what is lost when hard-to-place kidneys fail to reach a taker, the other that the investigation most often used to justify declining them cannot bear that weight. UK units that obtain pre-implantation biopsies on marginal offers should read this as a reason to record the histology alongside the clinical variables and the outcome rather than to act on it in isolation.

### 4. [Evaluation of eculizumab for the prevention of delayed graft function after kidney transplantation in adults: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.09.024)
[Marks WH, Patel A, Viklicky O, Glotz D, Ratner LE, Vincenti F, Cruzado JM, Galijasevic ST, Jiang X, Ogawa M, Haller H, Moreso F, Nguefouet Momo RE, Formica RN, Gill JS, Irish W. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42763038.]{.kw-ref}

Complement activation is a well-characterised component of ischaemia-reperfusion injury, and terminal pathway blockade at the moment of reperfusion has been the most biologically plausible candidate for preventing delayed graft function, which remains without any approved therapy while its incidence climbs on the back of expanded criteria donor use. This randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT02145182) gave adults aged 18 or over either eculizumab 1200 mg or placebo immediately before transplantation and either eculizumab 900 mg or placebo 18 to 24 hours afterwards, randomising 142 to eculizumab and 146 to placebo, with delayed graft function defined conventionally as the need for dialysis within the first seven days. It did not work: delayed graft function occurred in 51 of 142 (35.9%) eculizumab recipients against 60 of 144 (41.7%) placebo recipients, a treatment difference of −5.75% whose 95% confidence interval (−17.03% to 5.52%) comfortably crosses zero. Safety was unremarkable, with no substantial differences between the treatment groups, which is worth recording given the infectious risk that terminal complement blockade carries. Post hoc analysis found a −17.8% difference in delayed graft function favouring eculizumab among recipients of an expanded criteria donor kidney managed with static cold storage, a subgroup where the injury mechanism the drug targets would be expected to dominate — but this is a post hoc subgroup in a trial that missed its primary endpoint, and the correct reading is hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing. What a UK consultant should take from this is largely negative and largely useful: delayed graft function is not going to be prevented pharmacologically on current evidence, so the levers that remain are the ones this issue's other papers describe, namely preservation strategy, cold ischaemic time and donor selection, and the interest in complement blockade should now be directed at a properly powered trial confined to the expanded criteria cold storage population rather than at off-label use.

### 5. [Real-time Quality Assessment of Donor Kidneys During Normothermic Machine Perfusion Using Perfusate and Urinary Biomarkers](https://doi.org/10.1097/TXD.0000000000002010)
[Slagter JS, Papamanoli A, Akram F, Azam MA, Stubbs A, Clahsen-van Groningen MC, Porte RJ, Minnee RC. *Transplant Direct*, 2026. PMID: 42770166.]{.kw-ref}

If normothermic perfusion is going to earn its place as a viability test rather than a preservation method, it needs a readout available while the kidney is still on the circuit, and this predefined secondary analysis of the normothermic arm of a Rotterdam randomised trial is the largest series to date to correlate such readouts with outcomes in kidneys that were all actually transplanted. Forty-one kidneys received two hours of end-ischemic normothermic perfusion after hypothermic machine perfusion, from donors with a median age of 65 years (IQR 58–72), 30 of 41 (73%) donation after circulatory death, with a median cold ischaemia time of 9.5 hours and recipients of median age 67; delayed graft function occurred in 20 of 41 (49%), primary non-function in 3 (7%) and biopsy-proven rejection within two weeks in 5 (12%). After excluding the primary non-function cases a priori, the remaining 38 were split 70/30, with all feature selection confined to the 26-case training set to avoid leakage. Two signals emerged there: venous oxygen tension at 60 minutes was higher in kidneys that went on to delayed function (median 40.7 mm Hg, IQR 35.43–44.87, versus 32.0, 21.98–35.70; Cliff's delta 0.54, p = 0.022, AUC 0.77), and cumulative urine production over two hours was higher in those with immediate function (547.6 ± 328.9 versus 292.1 ± 156.6 mL; Hedges' g −0.99, p = 0.026), with the 120-minute value discriminating best (AUC 0.81). Urinary phosphate at 120 minutes did not reach significance (4 mg/dL, IQR 2.63–4.45, versus 3.1, 2.30–3.77; p = 0.16) but met the prespecified effect-size threshold and was retained, and the resulting three-feature penalised logistic regression achieved an out-of-fold AUC of 0.76 in training and 0.81 with 83% accuracy in a held-out test set of twelve. The higher venous oxygen tension in failing kidneys is the interesting mechanistic point, since at comparable flow and haemoglobin it implies reduced oxygen extraction, which the authors attribute variously to lower solute load and reduced tubular reabsorptive demand, impaired mitochondrial capacity, or heterogeneous intrarenal perfusion, and they concede the measurement cannot distinguish between these. Their own limitations are severe enough to govern interpretation: twelve kidneys in the test set, no adjustment for donor age, cold ischaemia time or donation type, delayed graft function a poor surrogate for viability in donation after circulatory death kidneys specifically, and readouts that are protocol-dependent because urine was recirculated and perfusate composition varies between centres, so coefficients and thresholds are specific to this circuit. For UK units running or commissioning normothermic perfusion, the transferable finding is which physiological axes to instrument — urine output, oxygen handling and solute handling — rather than any number in this paper, and the authors are right that external validation and decision-impact testing must come before a perfusion readout is allowed to decline an organ.

### 6. [Balancing Benefits and Risks: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of ABO-Incompatible Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.22037/uj.v23i04.8853)
[Pour-Rezagholi F, Samadian F, Hoseini Chimeh M, Amini H, Heidary SS, Dalili N. *Urol J*, 2026. PMID: 42773768.]{.kw-ref}

ABO-incompatible living donor transplantation has moved from experiment to routine in UK practice, and the question is no longer whether it works but what it costs relative to a compatible transplant in the same programme. This PRISMA 2020 review searched PubMed, Scopus and Embase from 2010 through December 2024 for observational cohort and registry studies comparing ABO-incompatible recipients with centre-matched or concurrent ABO-compatible controls, appraising quality with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and pooling risk ratios under random- and fixed-effects models, ultimately synthesising 63 studies covering 5,852 incompatible and 47,950 compatible recipients. The immunological cost is unambiguous and falls where the biology predicts: overall rejection risk was higher with incompatibility (risk ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.17–1.40) and antibody-mediated rejection more than doubled (risk ratio 2.14, 1.48–3.09), while T cell-mediated rejection was comparable between groups (risk ratio 0.86, 0.72–1.04). Patient and graft survival estimates at one, three and ten years were broadly compatible between the two groups, which is the reassuring headline, but the five-year patient survival estimate diverged in favour of ABO-compatible transplantation (risk ratio 1.62, 1.13–2.32) — an isolated outlier between concordant three- and ten-year estimates that the authors flag rather than explain, and one that should probably be read as a feature of which cohorts reported which timepoints rather than as a real hazard confined to the fifth year. Surgical complications and postoperative bleeding were markedly higher in the incompatible group, which is the practical surgical finding and is consistent with the antibody removal and enhanced immunosuppression these recipients undergo. The limitations are those of the underlying literature rather than the synthesis: every included study was observational, screening was restricted to English-language publications, and the authors relegated meta-regression, publication bias assessment and confounding evaluation to supplementary material because the unadjusted data were too sparse to support them. For a UK surgeon the usable summary is that ABO-incompatible transplantation buys access to an otherwise unavailable living donor at the price of roughly double the antibody-mediated rejection risk and a materially higher early bleeding and reoperation burden, with long-term graft and patient survival that appear to converge — a trade worth making for most candidates, and worth quantifying at consent in those terms.

### 7. [Apixaban Use Before Kidney Transplantation: Is Reversal Necessary?](https://doi.org/10.1002/phar.70200)
[Cotiguala L, Przybylski A, Linberger L, Brokhof M, Kenyon N, Joyce C, Dierker M, Ferguson K, Rech MA, Trotter C, Aguirre O, Lopez-Soler RI. *Pharmacotherapy*, 2026. PMID: 42736533.]{.kw-ref}

More candidates now arrive for a deceased donor transplant on a direct oral anticoagulant than a decade ago, and the recipient coordinator's question at three in the morning — whether a patient who took apixaban eighteen hours ago needs four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate before knife to skin — has had no evidence behind it in either direction. This retrospective two-centre study identified adult kidney transplant recipients from January 2019 to September 2025 who had taken apixaban within 48 hours of surgery and stratified them by whether they received preoperative reversal, with surgical-bed bleeding within three days as the primary endpoint tested for one-sided non-inferiority against a 15% margin. Fifty recipients were included, 14 (28%) reversed and 36 (72%) not, with a median 21 hours (IQR 16–24) since the last known apixaban dose. Surgical-bed bleeding occurred in 7.1% of the reversed group and 5.6% of the unreversed group, a difference of 1.6% with an upper one-sided confidence bound of 21.5% (p = 0.11), which means the event rates were similar but the study was too small to formally establish non-inferiority against its own margin. Nothing else separated the groups either: transfusion requirement, delayed graft function, kidney function, reoperation and venous thromboembolism (one event in the reversal group, none in the unreversed group) were all comparable, and the two deaths in the cohort both occurred among those who were reversed. Fifty patients across two centres and six years, retrospectively assembled with treatment assignment by clinician judgement, is a sample that cannot exclude a clinically meaningful difference, and confounding by indication runs in the obvious direction since the patients chosen for reversal were presumably those judged higher risk. Still, this is the largest series addressing the question, and it supports what many UK units already do by instinct — that with a documented dose interval approaching a day, individualised assessment rather than routine prothrombin complex concentrate is defensible, and the thrombotic risk and cost of reflexive reversal are real enough to make the default worth reconsidering.

### 8. [Early BK Polyomavirus-Specific Immunity and Viral Clearance](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2026.107064)
[Bertrand D, De Nattes T, Laurent C, Lemoine M, Lebourg L, Hanoy M, Le Roy F, Grangé S, Mauger E, Becquet A, Gueudin M, Guerrot D, Candon S. *Kidney Int Rep*, 2026. PMID: 42787867.]{.kw-ref}

BK management is currently a viral load and a guess: the load tells you the virus is replicating but not whether this particular recipient can control it, so immunosuppression comes down empirically and some patients are pushed into rejection unnecessarily while others are not reduced far enough. This single-centre French cohort tested whether measuring the host side at the outset changes the picture, performing a BK-specific interferon-gamma ELISPOT a median 17.4 days (IQR 11.1–35.2) after the first positive plasma PCR in 50 consecutive adult kidney-only recipients, drawn from 95 patients who developed viraemia among 568 transplants performed between 2020 and 2025, and quantifying responses separately against structural capsid antigens (VP1–VP3) and regulatory antigens (large T and small t). Structural responses varied enormously — median 100 spot-forming cells per million peripheral blood mononuclear cells (IQR 46–317.8, range 0 to 1,931) — and correlated only very weakly with peak viral load, which is the finding that makes the assay potentially additive rather than redundant. Thirty-seven of 50 (74%) cleared the virus, at a median 143 days (IQR 97–338) from the ELISPOT, and each additional 100 spot-forming cells was independently associated with faster clearance (adjusted hazard ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.15–1.42, p < 0.0001) after adjustment for viral load, immunosuppression intensity, age and time from transplant, and with a reduced need for deep immunosuppression reduction (adjusted odds ratio 0.34 per 100 spot-forming cells, p = 0.018), an association that survived further adjustment for tacrolimus trough and mycophenolate dose. Biopsy-proven nephropathy developed in 9 (18%) and their structural responses were far lower (median 25, IQR 0–43, versus 208.9, 61–328), though the adjusted association lost significance with so few events (odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.03–1.20, p = 0.076); receiver operating characteristic areas were 0.82 for clearance within 90 days, 0.84 for avoiding deep reduction and 0.86 for absence of nephropathy, with exploratory thresholds around 171 and 45 spot-forming cells. Responses to regulatory antigens were weaker and less consistent throughout, and creatinine trajectories tracked the same gradient, rising a median 12 µmol/L in those below the structural threshold and falling 6 µmol/L in those above, against a rise of 116 µmol/L in those who developed nephropathy. The authors are appropriately restrained about what this supports: a retrospective single-centre study using a locally developed and externally unstandardised assay, in which 46% of patients had already had mycophenolate reduced before the test, so the measurement is not a true baseline, and biopsies were clinically indicated rather than protocol-driven, meaning nephropathy was almost certainly under-ascertained. They explicitly reject replacing serial PCR monitoring with immune monitoring, and so should we — but for a UK unit the direction of travel is clear enough that the question worth asking is whether a validated, standardised BK ELISPOT should be commissioned alongside viral load monitoring, since the patients it would identify are precisely the ones in whom the current empirical reduction is either too timid or too aggressive.
